summary: Background: Machine learning has been extensively applied in medical prediction; however, existing machine-assisted pharmacotherapy review systems predominantly rely on structured, codifiable data while neglecting unstructured natural language clinical narratives, thereby allowing latent medication risks to remain undetected. Objective: To address the limitations of structured data–based review, this study proposes and validates a machine learning framework grounded in text classification for the automated identification of “prophylactic” vs “nonprophylactic” medication indications within clinical narratives. As a result, it aims to assist in the automated detection of prophylactic indication mentions for stress-related mucosal disease in clinical narratives as a preliminary step toward comprehensive medication-use review. Methods: A total of 3695 progress notes were independently annotated by 2 clinical pharmacists to construct a binary dataset for classifying prophylactic medication indication for stress-related mucosal disease, yielding an interannotator agreement κ of 0.8934. Comparative experiments were conducted using traditional machine learning models, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, CatBoost, and LightGBM, alongside TextCNN and a Chinese pretrained BERT model. The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets on a patient-wise basis, and model evaluation was conducted on the independent test set. SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis was used to achieve model interpretability and elucidate decision-making processes, ultimately enabling automated indication detection of prophylactic proton pump inhibitor administration. Results: All models and strategies demonstrated efficacy in medical text classification tasks. In a single-center cohort of 66 patients (3695 notes, 11.0% positive), the CatBoost model with balanced class weights achieved a note-level -score of 0.727 (precision=0.693; recall=0.765) and a patient-level -score of 0.889 (precision=0.800; recall=1.000) on the independent test set. At the note level, CatBoost achieved a higher -score than TextCNN (-score=0.718) and BERT (-score=0.628). Conclusions: In summary, the text classifier constructed through machine learning and natural language processing effectively extracts prophylactic medication indications for stress-related mucosal disease from unstructured progress notes. Combined with patient-level data partitioning, standardized annotation protocols, and an ethics-compliant framework, this approach provides an interpretable preliminary screening tool for identifying potential prophylactic indications to support subsequent pharmacist adjudication. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2600126317; https://tinyurl.com/yjzjd443
title: Machine Learning–Based Detection of Prophylactic Indication Mentions for Stress-Related Mucosal Disease in Chinese Clinical Progress Notes: Text Classification Study

summary: Background: Continuous patient monitoring generates vast volumes of high-frequency monitoring data, such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and invasive blood pressure tracings, that are often persisted in heterogeneous, noninteroperable formats, limiting integration with electronic health records and secondary use. Although Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) supports general health data exchange, native support for high-frequency medical monitoring data, including associated metadata and data quality metrics, remains limited. Objective: This study aims to develop a modality-agnostic FHIR package implementing a pattern to enable scalable, semantically precise representation of high-frequency medical monitoring data, decoupling structured clinical metadata from raw signal storage. Methods: This study provides the FHIR package Time Series Integration and Data in Endpoints (TIDE), a collection of FHIR Release 4 artifacts for interoperable exchange and the standardization of high-frequency monitoring clinical data, using electroencephalography as the primary use case while remaining applicable to generic medical monitoring data. The core TIDE profile separates technical metadata and analytical summaries stored directly in FHIR from high-volume raw data referenced via resources. Quantitative results are standardized with pattern slicing, including sampling frequency, statistical summaries, and data quality metrics. Semantic interoperability was achieved through a hybrid terminology binding, using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms, Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes for modalities, and custom for technical metadata, waveform modalities, channel identifiers, and connection types not covered by standard terminologies. All profiles were authored in FHIR Shorthand and compiled with SUSHI to produce a validated Implementation Guide conformant with the FHIR Release 4 core specification. Results: The resulting framework provides a modality-agnostic structure for high-frequency monitoring data, comprising 7 primary FHIR artifacts that define 16 distinct component slices for metadata and signal analysis results. resources reference associated and instances, encapsulate acquisition parameters, and link to full-time-series repositories. Controlled vocabularies ensure unambiguous exchange, thereby enabling downstream use in research and decision support. The architecture decouples the metadata layer from the storage layer via a standardized extension, enabling efficient querying of signals without retrieving large amounts of raw high-frequency monitoring data. Conclusions: TIDE provides a reusable, standards-compliant framework for integrating continuous high-frequency monitoring data into FHIR-based ecosystems. By separating semantically rich, queryable metadata from raw signal storage, TIDE enables longitudinal patient monitoring and automated signal quality-based triage without requiring modification of existing signal storage infrastructure.
title: Exchange of High-Frequency Medical Monitoring Data Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources for Interoperable Integration Into Clinical Practice and Research: Methodological Development Study

summary: Background: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classifies chronic kidney disease (CKD) using categories based on both glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria. Structured measures remain essential but may not capture contextual clinical concerns documented in narrative records. Objective: This study examined whether text-derived clinical-status language features in clinician notes were associated with deterioration in renal function in independent Greek- and English-language clinical cohorts. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed a Greek general-nephrology cohort (314 patients; 10,306 estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] measurements) and an independent English-language Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) replication cohort. The Greek primary analysis used a linear mixed effects model over a follow-up period of up to 1797 days. The MIMIC-IV primary analysis used a 90-day, patient-level fixed-horizon competing-outcome model (N=87,533). Separate analyses of Greek and MIMIC-IV data evaluated discrimination, calibration, and sensitivity to alternative feature specifications. Results: In the Greek cohort, a 1-SD higher negativity was associated with lower eGFR (=−3.273 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI −5.049 to −1.498; <.001) and a more negative time trajectory (time-by-score =−1.324, 95% CI −2.553 to −0.096; =.035). In MIMIC-IV, a 1-SD higher negative-vs-reassuring polarity contrast was associated with renal deterioration (relative risk ratio [RRR]=1.090, 95% CI 1.070‐1.110; <.001). Within eGFR G categories, polarity-score areas under the curve (AUCs) were 0.506 to 0.552 using discharge eGFR and 0.518 to 0.534 using the worst observed eGFR. Discrimination for renal deterioration remained modest (one-vs-rest AUC=0.6134, 95% CI 0.6092‐0.6175), and adding both natural language processing (NLP) features to the clinical model increased AUC by only 0.0018 (95% CI 0.0010‐0.0025). Conclusions: Independently constructed clinical-language measures were associated with renal function deterioration across two languages and health care settings. The findings support cross-language replication of an association signal, not formal external validation, measurement equivalence, or clinically useful stand-alone prediction.
title: Context-Dependent Clinical Narrative Signals of Renal Function Deterioration in Cross-Language Settings: Retrospective Multicohort Study

summary: Background: The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application. Objective: This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective. Methods: A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression. Results: The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI, ²=0.759), 67% in perceived usefulness (PU, ²=0.670), and 54% in perceived risk (PR, ²=0.540). PU showed the strongest positive association with BI (=.670, <.001, ²=0.457), whereas PR showed a small negative association (=−.149, =.04, ²=0.034). Transparency was positively associated with PU (=.220, =.001) and perceived ease of use (PEOU; =.454, <.001) and negatively associated with PR (=−.594, <.001). Perceived need (PN) showed a strong positive association with PU (=.567, <.001) but no significant direct association with BI (=.071, =.35). Eight of 20 hypotheses were supported. Only 23.5% (n=35) of participants reported actual ePA use. BI showed a positive but imprecise and nonsignificant association with self-reported actual use (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.89-2.11, =.15). Measurement quality was mixed: reflective constructs generally showed satisfactory reliability and convergent validity; however, discriminant validity between PU and BI was poor (heterotrait-monotrait ratio of correlations [HTMT]=0.981). Conclusions: PU showed the strongest association with behavioral intention in the ePA case evaluation, while transparency and PN were mainly associated with behavioral intention through indirect pathways. The findings suggest potential value in extending traditional acceptance models with governance-related constructs relevant to HDSs. However, the severe overlap between PU and behavioral intention, low actual ePA uptake, and the young, highly educated convenience sample limit confidence in the magnitude and distinctiveness of the observed effects. HDS-TAM should therefore be regarded as a promising but preliminary framework requiring further refinement and validation.
title: Health Dataspace Technology Acceptance Model (HDS-TAM): Development and Case Evaluation Study of Patient Acceptance of Germany’s Electronic Patient Record

summary: Background: Rare genetic diseases often present with recognizable facial phenotypes. Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can prioritize the diagnosis of rare genetic diseases from facial images and whether image enhancement or visual prompting can improve this process remain unclear. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MLLMs for rare genetic diseases using facial images and to assess whether super-resolution enhancement or red-circle visual prompting improved performance. Methods: This diagnostic accuracy study used 4746 facial images from the GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB), including 882 images in GMDB-Frequent from diseases with at least 6 images and 3864 images in GMDB-Rare from diseases with fewer than 6 images. Three locally deployed open-weight MLLMs—Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.8-27B—generated 50 ranked candidate diagnoses under raw image, CodeFormer-enhanced, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511–generated red-circle–prompted, mismatched red-circle, and 2-stage image-to-phenotype conditions. Candidate diagnoses were mapped to Mondo Disease Ontology (MONDO) identifiers. In addition, we evaluated a random baseline, visual-prompt quality, expert-annotated regions, repeated-inference stability, model-reported confidence, diagnostic-list perplexity, prediction overlap, and disease composition. Results: Top-50 accuracy ranged from 13.95% to 18.25% in GMDB-Frequent and from 0.57% to 1.35% in GMDB-Rare. Red-circle prompting produced numerical accuracy increases in 5 of 6 model-subset comparisons. Qwen3.8-27B showed a significant improvement in GMDB-Rare, with accuracy increasing from 0.57% to 1.27% (adjusted P=.009). In the good visual-prompt subgroup of GMDB-Frequent, Gemma-4-31B showed significant improvements over the super-resolution condition in both physician-rated analyses, with accuracy increases of 5.76 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.005) and 4.46 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.048), respectively. Matched red-circle inputs yielded higher accuracy than mismatched inputs across all model-subset comparisons, with adjusted P>.05. The image-to-phenotype workflow improved accuracy for Gemma-4-31B in GMDB-Frequent and Qwen3.8-27B in GMDB-Rare. In GMDB-Rare, the random baseline achieved 8.15% accuracy and exceeded all 3 models under the raw image and red-circle conditions. Prediction sets remained substantially overlapping after patient-image replacement, and top-1 predictions concentrated on a small number of diseases. Conclusions: Under the evaluated experimental settings, the 3 MLLMs showed limited ability to diagnose rare genetic diseases from facial images, particularly diseases in GMDB-Rare. Visual prompting and image-to-phenotype diagnosis produced benefits in specific models and subgroups. The prediction-overlap, mismatched-image, and disease-composition analyses indicate that model outputs were only weakly constrained by patient-specific facial information. Further studies should evaluate physician comparisons, prospective multicenter data, and phenotype-grounded multimodal diagnostic workflows.
title: Diagnosing Rare Genetic Diseases From Facial Images Using Visual Prompting With Multimodal Large Language Models: Diagnostic Accuracy Study

summary: Background: Accurate diagnosis of middle ear diseases remains challenging due to the specialized nature of otoscopic interpretation and the global shortage of otolaryngologists. Objective: We aimed to evaluate the impact of a deep learning–based AI support system on the diagnostic performance of clinicians with varying levels of expertise, specifically focusing on its ability to bridge the gap between trainees and experts. Methods: In this retrospective reader study, a deep learning model (EfficientNet-B4) was developed using a large-scale dataset of 7335 endoscopic images. The model was designed for multi-class classification, simultaneously identifying primary categories (chronic otitis media, otitis media with effusion, or none [indicating the absence of the first two]) and secondary features (attic retraction, myringitis, otomycosis, and ventilation tube). To assess clinical impact, diagnostic performance was compared among 3 otology professors, 5 senior residents, and 5 junior residents using an independent clinical assessment set of 100 images. Participants performed diagnoses both with and without AI-generated predictions, with a time constraint of 1 minute per image to simulate real-world clinical pressure. Results: In 5-fold cross-validation, the deep learning model achieved 94.8% accuracy for the primary classification. The stand-alone AI achieved diagnostic accuracies ranging from 94.0% to 99.0% in the clinical assessment set. AI support significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy across all groups for primary classification, with improvements of 11.0% for otology professors, 28.8% for senior residents, and 32.2% for junior residents (<.001). Accuracy increased from 78.7% to 89.7% for otology professors, from 65.0% to 93.8% for senior residents, and from 54.4% to 86.6% for junior residents. The accuracy gap between the most experienced (otology professors) and least experienced (junior residents) groups was reduced from 24.3% to 3.1%. For secondary categories, significant improvements were observed in diagnosing attic retraction and myringitis among residents. AI-supported accuracy for attic retraction was higher in senior residents than that of the stand-alone AI, although the 95% CIs overlapped substantially, so the difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate that deep learning–based AI support substantially improves the diagnostic accuracy of middle ear diseases, particularly for less experienced clinicians. By narrowing the performance gap between trainees and experts, this system shows high potential as a valuable adjunct for clinical decision-making and medical education in otology.
title: Deep Learning–Assisted Diagnosis of Middle Ear Diseases in Otoendoscopy Across Clinician Experience Levels: Retrospective Reader Study

summary: Background: Many digital health and AI initiatives show promising results in pilot settings but do not progress to sustainable services. Pilots can operate within a predefined collaboration, whereas operational services must accommodate changes in participating organizations, available resources, and analytical capabilities while preserving established governance and technical arrangements. Objective: This study examines the pilot-to-service transition as a problem of governed federation evolution and evaluates whether Open Health can admit new forms of participation while preserving bounded capabilities, organizational sovereignty, and auditable decision evidence. Methods: Open Health applies federated computing (FC) as a governance model separated from the analytical runtime. A governed federation context is established before execution, participants receive holder-bound capabilities, and an admission gateway produces explicit ALLOW or DENY decisions before requested operations proceed. The proof of concept uses the Flower federated learning framework and the Pathology Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (PathMNIST) dataset from the MedMNIST collection with an initial federation comprising hospitals A and B. Mode 1A introduces hospital C as a sponsored contributor permitted to submit locally computed training updates but not invoke the resulting federated model for inference. Mode 1B examines bounded AI-agent participation, where restricted results may be transformed through policy-authorized operations into derivatives whose consumption is governed independently from the source. Evaluation considers admission conformance, signed decision evidence, analytical effects of the additional contribution, and admission overhead. Results: The demonstrator admitted valid member operations and hospital C’s sponsored contribution (mode 1A) while denying model consumption outside hospital C’s capability, scope violations, holder-binding mismatch, and federation-envelope mismatch. Mode 1B extended the same bounded-governance pattern to AI-agent participation, admitting bounded inference and governed transformation but denying unauthorized source consumption and privileged governance access. Under matched training conditions, cancer-related macro recall increased from 50.2% in the A+B control to 67.4% in A+B+C (+17.2 percentage points), while noncancer macro recall changed from 85.5% to 86.3% (+0.8 percentage points). Recall increased from 19.5% to 39.9% for cancer-associated stroma and from 80.9% to 94.9% for colorectal adenocarcinoma epithelium. Median (IQR) full admission latency was 1.210 (1.141-1.333) ms for ALLOW, 1.195 (1.136-1.273) ms for capability-scope DENY, and 0.884 (0.837-0.921) ms for holder-binding DENY. Each evaluated request generated signed decision evidence recording the decision, reason, participant and request bindings, governance context, and related model run. Conclusions: Open Health demonstrates how a federated health-data collaboration can evolve through differentiated participation while preserving membership boundaries and bounded capability relations. The principal contribution is an executable governance boundary preserving capability relations and producing independently verifiable decision evidence separately from the federated-learning runtime. The analytical experiment showed that governed admission of an additional contributor produced a measurable effect on the intended cancer-related classes while preserving noncancer performance. The proof of concept establishes governance behavior under controlled conditions; clinical effectiveness and production-scale performance require further evaluation.
title: Admission Mechanisms for Scalable Federated Health Data Collaboration: Design and Proof-of-Concept Study

summary: Background: Electronic health record–derived process measures such as vital-sign record density are used for quality monitoring, risk prediction, and cross-system benchmarking, but whether they retain consistent meaning across sites and data streams is rarely tested. Objective: This study aimed to determine whether vital-sign record density varies primarily by data stream, database, contributing site, or care unit, and what follows for comparative use. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) version 3.1 and the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) version 2.0. Record density and timing metrics were computed for the first 24 intensive care unit hours from nurse-charted streams and, in eICU-CRD, from the monitor stream. Heart rate was primary; oxygen saturation and respiratory rate were replication variables. Variance was decomposed by database, hospital, and unit using η2 with hospital-clustered bootstrap inference and mixed-effects sensitivity analyses. A hospital-level plausibility floor of 12 nurse-charted heart rate observations per 24 hours was applied for the principal analysis; unrestricted and alternative-floor analyses are reported as sensitivities. Results: A pooled-item MIMIC-IV heart rate count included alarm-limit documentation events, so label-based pooling mixes the two. In 117,572 eICU-CRD stays present in both streams, nurse- and monitor-derived counts were almost unrelated (Spearman ρ=0.024), with bottom-decile overlap at chance. Between-database η2 for record count was 0.960 against the eICU monitor stream and 0.026 against the nurse stream. Eight of 68 eICU-CRD hospitals fell below the plausibility floor and were excluded from principal estimates, a restriction introduced during review. Among the remaining 60 hospitals (88,560 stays), hospital η2 for record count was 0.354 (95% CI 0.259-0.450) against unit-within-hospital η2 of 0.043; for the interval-structure metrics, the hospital and unit components were not separable. For record count, the hospital component fell from 0.441 unrestricted to 0.321 at an hourly floor. A negative-binomial mixed model gave latent-scale hospital and unit variance-partition coefficients of 0.348 (95% CI 0.252-0.457) and 0.112 (0.078-0.163), equivalent to 0.318 and 0.110 observed. A pooled bottom-decile rule agreed with hospital-specific rules on 52.5% (4726/9006) of flagged stays, with 6 hospitals supplying half the pooled decile. The hospital component for record count replicated at 0.322 for oxygen saturation and 0.333 for respiratory rate. Conclusions: Within a multisite nurse-charted stream, vital-sign record volume varied more across contributing sites than across care units within hospitals; for the interval-structure metrics, the site and unit components were not separable at this cohort size. Apparent cross-database differences were reproduced by source-table choice, and site-level variation remained after excluding the most evident contribution-completeness outliers. Comparative use therefore requires specifying the generating stream, enforcing the analytic window, and explicitly modeling site-level variation; the residual site component should not be interpreted as documentation practice alone.
title: Data Stream and Hospital-Level Variation in Intensive Care Unit Vital-Sign Record Density Across Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV and eICU Collaborative Research Database: Retrospective Data Quality Study

summary: Background: Frailty is prevalent among hospitalized patients and is associated with increased risk of complications, prolonged hospitalization, higher mortality, and health care costs. Existing frailty screening tools, including the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS), have limitations related to subjectivity, resource intensity, or reliance on retrospective data, limiting their use in routine acute care. Early identification of frailty is critical to support targeted interventions and resource allocation, yet scalable approaches for predicting frailty early during hospital admission remain limited. Objective: This paper evaluates whether routinely collected electronic medical record (EMR) data available within the first 72 hours of admission can be used to predict frailty in hospitalized patients. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using routinely collected EMR data from the Royal Adelaide Hospital (RAH), including overnight admissions with a length of stay of at least 72 hours between July 2023 and December 2024. Frailty was defined using the HFRS (score >4). Predictors were derived from EMR data available within 72 hours of admission, including demographics, medications, laboratory results, nursing assessments, and medical and allied health consult orders. Data were split into training (21,436/26,824, 80%) and test (5388/26,824, 20%) sets. Multiple machine learning models were trained, with the -score as the primary optimization metric. Model performance was evaluated using the -score, recall, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), calibration, and clinical utility analyses. Results: This study included 26,824 admissions, of whom 9427 (35%) were classified as frail. The final XGBoost (XGB) model achieved an -score of 0.755 (95% CI 0.741-0.768), an AUROC of 0.777 (95% CI 0.764-0.790), and a recall of 0.873 (95% CI 0.857-0.887) on the test dataset, with good calibration and an expected-to-observed ratio close to 1 (0.996, 95% CI 0.963-1.028). Key predictors included polypharmacy, laboratory results (including creatinine, albumin, and sodium), allied health consult orders, and nursing assessment data. Model performance was lower at 24 hours postadmission and improved by discharge. Conclusions: An EMR-based frailty prediction model using data available at 72 hours postadmission can identify patients with frailty early in their hospital stay, supporting targeted interventions and operational planning. Reduced performance in Indigenous patients highlights the need for culturally validated frailty indices and ongoing evaluation of equity in predictive modeling.
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Electronic Medical Record–Based Machine Learning Model for Frailty Prediction in Hospitalized Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Background: Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder characterized by high disability and relapse rates, posing significant challenges to public safety and community-based mental health management. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a model for identifying hospitalization-related severe relapse risk among individuals with schizophrenia and to determine the key factors associated with this risk. Methods: A total of 44,804 electronic records of community-managed individuals with schizophrenia were extracted from an information management system between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2023. The dataset included demographic information, clinical records, interview data, policy support, and management indicators to construct a comprehensive feature system. A Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) machine learning algorithm was used for model development, with cost-sensitive learning applied to address class imbalance. Model interpretability was enhanced using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to identify the most influential predictors of relapse risk. Results: After screening, a total of 39,818 community-dwelling individuals with schizophrenia were included in this study, of whom 3717 (9.33%) experienced hospitalization-related severe relapse. The dataset was randomly divided using stratified sampling into a training set (n=31,854, 80%) and an independent test set (n=7964, 20%). Among the 6 machine learning models evaluated, LightGBM showed leading and balanced performance, yielding an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.95, an area under the precision–recall curve of 0.79, a relapse-class recall of 0.77, a precision of 0.71, and an -score of 0.74 in the independent test set. SHAP-based interpretability analysis identified medication persistence (23.30%), specialist recommendation: medication adherence training (19.74%), number of follow-ups (7.38%), age (3.72%), and educational attainment (3.58%) as the most influential predictors. Higher hospitalization-related severe relapse risk was generally associated with interrupted or refused medication use, more frequent follow-ups, younger age, and higher educational attainment, whereas sustained medication use, better occupational functioning and productive work, greater social participation, and better social functioning were associated with lower predicted risk. Conclusions: This study developed a hospitalization-related severe relapse risk identification model that integrates multidimensional factors reflecting the clinical and functional complexity of schizophrenia. The findings provide an evidence-based foundation for risk identification, targeted intervention, and the optimization of community mental health services to reduce hospitalization-related severe relapse risk and support long-term recovery.
title: Analysis and Prediction of Relapse Risk Factors in Community-Dwelling Individuals With Schizophrenia: Retrospective Cohort Study
